$comment: AUROS containers-policy.json -- installed to /etc/containers/policy.json by
build/30-update-agent.sh. @AUROS_SCOPE@ is substituted at build time from AUROS_SCOPE,
which derives from auros.config.json (D1: the namespace lives in exactly one file).
D8, and this is the whole point of the file: deriving from Aurora gives us NOTHING here.
The stock policy has a global default of insecureAcceptAnything, so `bootc switch
--enforce-container-sigpolicy` succeeds while verifying nothing at all.
HOW SCOPE PRECEDENCE ACTUALLY WORKS, because 'put it before the catch-all' is the intent
but not the mechanism. JSON objects are unordered and containers/image does not read them
in order. From containers-policy.json(5): 'If multiple policy requirements match a given
image, only the requirements from the MOST SPECIFIC match apply, the more general policy
requirement definitions are ignored.' So the ghcr.io/<ns> entry below wins over the ""
catch-all for our images because it is a longer scope, not because of where it sits in the
file. Moving it would change nothing; deleting it would silently disable enforcement.
WHY THE CATCH-ALL STAYS. Setting transports.docker[""] to reject would break distrobox,
toolbox and every other image a user legitimately pulls. The deliberate, documented trade
is: OUR namespace is enforced, everything else is the same as any Fedora desktop.
signing/verify-enforcement.sh (check U4) is what proves the specific entry actually beats
the catch-all, by offering an UNSIGNED image inside our own namespace and requiring refusal.
WHY default IS reject AND NOT insecureAcceptAnything. bootc's enforce-container-sigpolicy
checks the GLOBAL default only -- see is_default_insecure() in bootc's
crates/ostree-ext/src/container/skopeo.rs. With the stock Fedora default, that guard fails.
With reject, it passes, and non-docker transports are re-permitted individually below.
signedIdentity matchRepository is MANDATORY, not decorative: cosign signatures carry only a
repository, and the default matchExact would reject every signature we ever make. If it were
missing, every pull would fail -- including the good ones -- and a negative test that only
checks 'the bad image was refused' would pass vacuously. That is why verify-enforcement.sh
runs a positive control first and aborts as INCONCLUSIVE if the good image is refused.
